papers.title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety lies at the core of developing and deploying large language models (LLMs). However, previous safety benchmarks only concern the safety in one language, e.g. the majority language in the pretraining data such as English. In this work, we build the first multilingual safety benchmark for LLMs, XSafety, in response to the global deployment of LLMs in practice. XSafety covers 14 kinds of commonly used safety issues across 10 languages that span several language families. We utilize XSafety to empirically study the multilingual safety for 4 widely-used LLMs, including both close-API and open-source models. Experimental results show that all LLMs produce significantly more unsafe responses for non-English queries than English ones, indicating the necessity of developing safety alignment for non-English languages. In addition, we propose several simple and effective prompting methods to improve the multilingual safety of ChatGPT by evoking safety knowledge and improving cross-lingual generalization of safety alignment. Our prompting method can significantly reduce the ratio of unsafe responses from 19.1% to 9.7% for non-English queries. We release our data at https://github.com/Jarviswang94/Multilingual_safety_benchmark.

papers.title: Safety Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models
papers.abstract: With the rapid popularity of large language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, a growing amount of attention is paid to their safety concerns. These models may generate insulting and discriminatory content, reflect incorrect social values, and may be used for malicious purposes such as fraud and dissemination of misleading information. Evaluating and enhancing their safety is particularly essential for the wide application of large language models (LLMs). To further promote the safe deployment of LLMs, we develop a Chinese LLM safety assessment benchmark. Our benchmark explores the comprehensive safety performance of LLMs from two perspectives: 8 kinds of typical safety scenarios and 6 types of more challenging instruction attacks. Our benchmark is based on a straightforward process in which it provides the test prompts and evaluates the safety of the generated responses from the evaluated model. In evaluation, we utilize the LLM's strong evaluation ability and develop it as a safety evaluator by prompting. On top of this benchmark, we conduct safety assessments and analyze 15 LLMs including the OpenAI GPT series and other well-known Chinese LLMs, where we observe some interesting findings. For example, we find that instruction attacks are more likely to expose safety issues of all LLMs. Moreover, to promote the development and deployment of safe, responsible, and ethical AI, we publicly release SafetyPrompts including 100k augmented prompts and responses by LLMs.

papers.title: Safety at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey of Large Model and Agent Safety
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large models, driven by their exceptional abilities in learning and generalization through large-scale pre-training, has reshaped the landscape of Artificial Intelligence (AI). These models are now foundational to a wide range of applications, including conversational AI, recommendation systems, autonomous driving, content generation, medical diagnostics, and scientific discovery. However, their widespread deployment also exposes them to significant safety risks, raising concerns about robustness, reliability, and ethical implications. This survey provides a systematic review of current safety research on large models, covering Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and large-model-powered Agents. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We present a comprehensive taxonomy of safety threats to these models, including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, backdoor attacks, jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, energy-latency attacks, data and model extraction attacks, and emerging agent-specific threats. (2) We review defense strategies proposed for each type of attacks if available and summarize the commonly used datasets and benchmarks for safety research. (3) Building on this, we identify and discuss the open challenges in large model safety, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety evaluations, scalable and effective defense mechanisms, and sustainable data practices. More importantly, we highlight the necessity of collective efforts from the research community and international collaboration. Our work can serve as a useful reference for researchers and practitioners, fostering the ongoing development of comprehensive defense systems and platforms to safeguard AI models.

papers.title: Enhanced Diagnostic and Interpretable Model for Febrile Diseases Using Explainable AI and Large Language Model
papers.abstract: <p><span>Tropical febrile diseases pose significant public health challenges in tropical regions, particularly in resource-limited settings, where timely and accurate diagnoses are critical for effective disease management. However, existing diagnostic systems are black-box and often lack interpretability, making it difficult for healthcare practitioners to understand and trust machine learning (ML) predictions. Additionally, the existing system excludes younger patients, limiting its applicability. This study aimed to develop an integrated diagnostic system that enhances interpretability by leveraging machine learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), and a large language model (LLM). A dataset comprising 3,914 patient records with 32 symptoms was obtained from a New Frontiers in Research Fund-sponsored project and preprocessed for analysis. Random Forest (RF) was trained with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation to optimize its performance. The tuned model achieved high diagnostic performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in diagnosing six febrile diseases. To enhance interpretability, a Model Interpretability Framework (MIF) was incorporated, integrating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) for visual insights and ChatGPT for textual explanations. This combination provided users with a clear understanding of the diagnostic process, addressing the limitations of black-box ML models. The system was implemented using Python in a development environment that included Google Colaboratory, Visual Studio Code, Flet, and MySQL for database management. Agile development methodology and Unified Modeling Language tools were employed to create a user-friendly design for clinicians and patients. The diagnostic system was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics. The RF model achieved outstanding precision for most diseases, high recall (≥0.97), and an AUC-ROC of 0.99, indicating nearly flawless training performance with few misclassifications. On the test dataset, the model performed better in diagnosing malaria (F1-score = 88%, precision = 85%), urinary tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 80%), and respiratory tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 77%). The evaluated system demonstrated strong predictive performance, correctly identifying 72 out of 99 tested patient cases, with 26 cases misclassified and one case completely missed. It achieved the highest detection rates for Malaria and HIV/AIDS, accurately identifying all cases without false positives. This work enhances diagnostic solutions for tropical healthcare settings by improving explainability and ensuring inclusivity for younger patients, addressing key limitations in existing systems. The integration of ML, XAI, and LLM enhances diagnostic performance and lays the groundwork for future AI-driven healthcare innovations, ultimately improving health outcomes in resource-scarce regions. Healthcare providers should adopt this system to enhance the efficiency of disease diagnosis and extend the system to diagnose additional medical conditions.&nbsp;</span></p>

literature_themes.theme: Multilingual Safety and Assessment of Large Language Models
literature_themes.summary: This cluster of papers focuses on the safety assessment of large language models (LLMs) across different languages, highlighting the necessity for multilingual safety benchmarks and evaluations. It introduces tools like XSafety for assessing safety across multiple languages and develops specific benchmarks for Chinese LLMs. The studies reveal that LLMs tend to produce more unsafe responses in non-English queries and emphasize the importance of improving safety measures for diverse linguistic contexts.
literature_themes.limitations: The research primarily addresses safety in a limited number of languages and may not cover all potential safety issues or scenarios. Additionally, while benchmarks are developed, the effectiveness of proposed safety improvements may vary across different LLM architectures and applications.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster identifies a significant research gap in the multilingual safety of LLMs, suggesting a need for comprehensive safety assessments and improvements in non-English contexts. It provides a foundation for future research to enhance the safety and reliability of LLMs in diverse linguistic and cultural settings.

literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights the need for further exploration of the scalability and generalizability of language model-enhanced representations in various recommendation scenarios, thus identifying a gap for future research.

summary: The retrieved literature emphasizes the importance of multilingual safety assessments for large language models (LLMs), revealing significant safety risks in non-English contexts and advocating for interpretable safety mechanisms. Additionally, it explores the integration of LLMs in few-shot recommender systems, highlighting the need for improved representation and interpretability. Overall, the studies identify critical gaps in comprehensive safety evaluations and the generalizability of LLM-enhanced applications across diverse scenarios.
scholarly_positioning: Existing research has predominantly focused on the safety assessments of large language models (LLMs) in multilingual contexts, revealing significant gaps in interpretability and comprehensive safety mechanisms, particularly for non-English languages. While tools like XSafety have been developed, they lack depth in understanding the underlying safety mechanisms and their interpretability across diverse LLM architectures. Additionally, the integration of LLMs in few-shot recommender systems has highlighted the need for enhanced representation but has not sufficiently addressed the interpretability of these enhancements. This proposed research aims to bridge these gaps by developing interpretable internal representations that enhance both safety and controllability in LLMs, situating it within the broader discourse on ethical AI deployment and the necessity for robust, interpretable frameworks in diverse applications.
research_scope: This empirical study will focus on the multilingual safety assessment of large language models (LLMs) specifically targeting non-English language contexts, with an emphasis on Chinese LLMs. The intervention will involve the development and application of an interpretable safety assessment framework, utilizing the XSafety benchmark to evaluate safety across 10 languages over a study period of 12 months. A control group will consist of traditional safety evaluation methods currently used in LLM assessments. Primary outcomes will include the reduction of unsafe response rates in non-English queries, while secondary outcomes will assess the interpretability of safety mechanisms and user trust in the LLM outputs. This research aims to enhance both the safety and controllability of LLMs through interpretable internal representations.
gap: Prior studies have demonstrated significant safety risks in non-English contexts for large language models (LLMs), particularly in Chinese LLMs; however, they treat the interpretability of safety mechanisms as secondary, leaving unclear whether the lack of interpretability affects user trust and safety outcomes. This matters practically because enhancing interpretability could lead to more reliable and trusted LLM applications in multilingual settings; therefore, this study investigates the development of interpretable internal representations to improve safety and controllability in non-English LLMs within the defined scope.
question: How does the implementation of interpretable internal representations in Chinese large language models affect the safety outcomes and user trust compared to traditional safety evaluation methods over a 12-month period?
theoretical_mechanism: The proposed intervention of interpretable internal representations in Chinese large language models (LLMs) serves as the independent variable. This intervention is expected to enhance user trust (mediator) through improved understanding of safety mechanisms. The psychological mechanism involves users feeling more secure and informed when interacting with LLMs that provide interpretable outputs, which in turn influences their trust levels. The primary outcome is the reduction of unsafe response rates in non-English queries (dependent variable). The theoretical framework is grounded in the principles of interpretability in AI, suggesting that increased transparency leads to greater user confidence and safer interactions. Key assumptions requiring empirical validation include that enhanced interpretability directly correlates with increased user trust and that this trust leads to safer usage outcomes.
hypothesis: The implementation of interpretable internal representations in Chinese large language models will lead to a significant reduction in unsafe response rates in non-English queries compared to traditional safety evaluation methods, mediated by an increase in user trust over a 12-month period.
operationalization_causal_check:
Construct Operationalization Table:

| Construct Name                     | Role        | Measurement Instrument/Behavioral Log | Data Source                | Timing               |
|------------------------------------|-------------|--------------------------------------|---------------------------|----------------------|
| Interpretable Internal Representations | IV          | XSafety benchmark scores             | LLM outputs               | Monthly assessments   |
| User Trust                          | Mediator    | Trust survey (Likert scale)         | User feedback              | Quarterly surveys     |
| Unsafe Response Rates               | DV          | Response analysis logs               | LLM interaction data      | Monthly assessments   |

Causal Pathway:
The implementation of interpretable internal representations (IV) is expected to enhance user trust (mediator), which in turn will lead to a reduction in unsafe response rates (DV) in non-English queries.

Likely Confounds:
Potential confounding variables may include user familiarity with LLMs, prior experiences with LLM outputs, and external influences such as media coverage of AI safety issues.

Claim Boundaries:
The study can claim that enhanced interpretability leads to increased user trust and reduced unsafe responses in the context of Chinese LLMs. However, it cannot claim causation beyond the specific context of this study or generalize findings to all LLMs or languages without further research.

What Cannot Be Concluded:
The study cannot conclude that interpretability alone is the sole factor influencing user trust or safety outcomes, nor can it determine the long-term effects beyond the 12-month assessment period.
methodology: This study will employ a three-arm design involving a target intervention group utilizing interpretable internal representations in Chinese LLMs, an active control group using traditional safety evaluation methods, and a usual-care group for baseline comparisons. Participants will be recruited from diverse linguistic backgrounds to ensure representation across non-English contexts. The primary operationalized variables include the XSafety benchmark scores for safety assessment, user trust measured through a Likert scale survey, and unsafe response rates derived from interaction logs. Evaluation metrics will focus on the reduction of unsafe responses and the correlation with user trust over a 12-month period. Statistical analyses will include repeated measures ANOVA to assess differences between groups while controlling for potential confounds such as user familiarity with LLMs. The study will ensure reproducibility by adhering to standardized protocols for data collection and analysis, and will maintain scope control by focusing exclusively on Chinese LLMs and their safety outcomes.
novelty_contribution: Theoretically, this research introduces a novel framework for understanding the interplay between interpretability and user trust in the context of non-English large language models (LLMs), specifically in Chinese, thereby advancing the discourse on ethical AI deployment. Methodologically, it employs a rigorous three-arm design to empirically test the effects of interpretable internal representations on safety outcomes, utilizing the XSafety benchmark and user trust metrics, which has not been systematically explored in multilingual contexts. Practically, the study aims to create actionable insights for developers and policymakers by demonstrating how enhanced interpretability can lead to improved safety and user confidence in LLM applications, addressing significant gaps in current safety assessment practices. This contribution goes beyond simply applying AI techniques; it establishes a clear causal mechanism linking interpretability to user trust and safety, which is critical for the responsible deployment of AI technologies in diverse linguistic environments.

proposal: This research proposal aims to investigate the impact of interpretable internal representations on safety outcomes and user trust in Chinese large language models (LLMs) over a 12-month period, addressing the significant safety risks identified in non-English contexts, particularly for Chinese LLMs. Existing literature highlights a lack of interpretability in safety assessments, which is critical for enhancing user trust and ensuring safe interactions. The research question posits: How does the implementation of interpretable internal representations in Chinese LLMs affect safety outcomes and user trust compared to traditional safety evaluation methods? The theoretical mechanism suggests that interpretable internal representations (independent variable) enhance user trust (mediator), leading to a reduction in unsafe response rates (dependent variable). The hypothesis asserts that these representations will significantly reduce unsafe responses compared to traditional methods, mediated by increased user trust. Constructs will be operationalized through monthly assessments of XSafety benchmark scores, quarterly user trust surveys using a validated Likert scale, and analysis of unsafe response rates from interaction logs. A three-arm design will compare an intervention group utilizing interpretable representations, an active control group using traditional methods, and a usual-care group for baseline comparisons. The study's expected contributions include advancing theoretical understanding of interpretability in AI, employing a rigorous methodology to empirically test the effects of interpretability on safety, and providing actionable insights for developers and policymakers. Novelty lies in the integration of interpretability with user trust in non-English LLMs, an area underexplored in existing literature. Key limitations include potential misinterpretation of results, data sparsity, and confounding variables, which will be mitigated through comprehensive training, diverse recruitment, and controlled analyses, ensuring robust findings that contribute to the responsible deployment of AI technologies in diverse linguistic environments.
